body:
Tombs in Gujarat's Indo-Islamic architecture

Mosques were not the only important buildings commissioned during the Gujarat Sultanate. Rulers, royal families and influential religious figures were also commemorated through tombs and mausoleums.

A maqbara is a tomb or mausoleum. A dargah is a shrine associated with the grave of a Sufi saint. The term roza, as used in Gujarat, is commonly associated with a tomb or funerary shrine complex and may refer to a wider group of related buildings.

These terms are connected, but they do not all mean a mosque. A large roza complex may contain a mosque, one or more tombs, courtyards, water features and other buildings.

Badshah no Haziro: the tomb of Ahmad Shah

Badshah no Haziro, also called the King's Mausoleum, is the tomb complex of Ahmedabad's founder, Sultan Ahmad Shah I.

Constructed in 1446, it stands near Manek Chowk and the Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad.

Along with Ahmad Shah I, the mausoleum contains the graves of his son Muhammad Shah and grandson Qutb-ud-Din.

The building has a large central dome, smaller domed chambers, surrounding passages and finely carved stone screens. Its form demonstrates how Gujarat's regional architectural style was also used for royal funerary buildings.

Rani no Haziro: the queens' mausoleum

Rani no Haziro is the mausoleum complex associated with the queens of Ahmad Shah I. It lies near Badshah no Haziro in the Manek Chowk area.

The complex dates to the 15th century and contains a courtyard enclosed by delicate stonework and arcaded elements.

Rani no Haziro must be distinguished from Rani Sipri's tomb, which belongs to a separate mosque-and-tomb ensemble near Astodia Gate.

Sarkhej Roza: a larger religious and funerary complex

Sarkhej Roza lies southwest of Ahmedabad's old city. It is an important example of Gujarat's provincial Indo-Islamic architecture because it combines religious, funerary and other architectural functions.

The complex is associated with the Sufi saint Shaikh Ahmad Khattu Ganj Bakhsh, who was a spiritual adviser of Ahmad Shah I.

Shaikh Ahmad Khattu died in 1445. His tomb was commissioned under Sultan Muhammad Shah II and completed in 1451.

Later, Sultan Mahmud Begada expanded the complex, including its large tank and further royal structures.

The architecture of Sarkhej Roza

The complex contains several related elements:

  • The saint's mausoleum: the principal shrine associated with Shaikh Ahmad Khattu Ganj Bakhsh.
  • A mosque: a space for congregational worship.
  • Royal mausoleums: tombs associated with members of the Gujarat Sultanate's ruling family.
  • A large tank: a major water feature around which buildings are grouped.
  • Palace and pavilion structures: evidence of the site's association with royal patronage and retreat.

Stone jalis and carved architectural details are characteristic of the complex. Its extensive use of pillared and horizontally supported elements shows that a major Indo-Islamic monument could retain a strong trabeate character rather than relying mainly on large arches.

Comparing Ahmedabad's tomb traditions

MonumentAssociationImportant distinction
Badshah no HaziroAhmad Shah I and royal descendantsRoyal mausoleum near Jama Masjid
Rani no HaziroQueens of Ahmad Shah ISeparate queens' tomb complex near Manek Chowk
Rani Sipri's tombQueen Subha RaiPart of the mosque-and-tomb ensemble near Astodia Gate
Sarkhej RozaShaikh Ahmad Khattu and Gujarat Sultanate rulersSufi shrine, mosque, tombs and water tank

Prelims focus

  • Badshah no Haziro: tomb of Ahmad Shah I, constructed in 1446.
  • Rani no Haziro: mausoleum associated with the queens of Ahmad Shah I.
  • Sarkhej Roza: associated with Shaikh Ahmad Khattu Ganj Bakhsh.
  • The saint died in 1445; his tomb was completed in 1451.
  • Mahmud Begada expanded the Sarkhej complex.
  • Trap: Sarkhej Roza is a complex containing a mosque and tombs; the term does not identify only the mosque.

[Sources: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation Heritage Department, Badshah no Haziro, Rani no Haziro and Rani Sipri Tomb, monument descriptions, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Sarkhej Roza, About the Location and Brief History, consulted 23 November 2026; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 8, printed pp. 110–111 and 114–115.]

body:
What is a minaret?

A minaret is a tower associated with mosque architecture. Traditionally, minarets were linked with the azaan, or call to prayer. They also became prominent visual features of religious buildings and could express the prestige of a patron or city.

In Gujarat Sultanate architecture, minarets frequently appear as slender towers with elaborate stone carving. Some are attached to the façade of a mosque, often near its entrance. Projecting galleries or balconies may divide the tower into successive stages.

Local craftsmen used carved bands, brackets and decorative mouldings to give these towers a distinctive regional appearance.

How minarets differ from other mosque elements

A minaret is a vertical architectural feature, not a prayer niche or a dome. Its form should be distinguished from the following:

  • Mihrab: a niche indicating the direction of Mecca.
  • Dome: a curved roof covering an interior space.
  • Jali: a perforated screen placed in an opening or enclosure.
  • Minaret: a tower, often rising beside or above a mosque façade.

Jhulta Minara: the shaking minarets

Ahmedabad is famous for the Jhulta Minara, or Shaking Minarets. One particularly well-known surviving pair is associated with the Sidi Bashir Mosque near Sarangpur Darwaza.

These minarets belong to the Sultanate architectural tradition. They are known for their tall, slender appearance, multiple stages and finely carved projecting balconies.

The towers acquired their popular name because of reports that movement in one minaret caused a corresponding vibration in the other, while the connecting portion did not show the same obvious movement.

The precise structural explanation for the reported phenomenon is not established. It should therefore not be presented as proof of a particular earthquake-resistant technology or an intentionally designed vibration mechanism.

For heritage protection, demonstrations involving shaking the minarets are no longer carried out.

Minarets at other Gujarat monuments

Minarets also help distinguish the mosques of Ahmedabad and Champaner:

  • Ahmedabad Jama Masjid: originally possessed a prominent pair of façade minarets, but these were damaged.
  • Champaner Jama Masjid: has 2 tall central minarets associated with its monumental prayer-hall façade.
  • Champaner Nagina Masjid: retains carved lower portions of minarets beside its central arch.

These examples show why a mosque's present appearance must be interpreted carefully. A monument may never have possessed minarets, or it may have lost part of an earlier arrangement through damage.

Do not confuse a missing minaret with a damaged minaret. Champaner's Nagina Masjid retains carved lower portions of its minarets, while Ahmedabad's Jama Masjid has surviving remains of an originally more substantial minaret arrangement.

Prelims focus

  • Jhulta Minara means Shaking Minarets.
  • The famous pair near Sarangpur is associated with Sidi Bashir Mosque, Ahmedabad.
  • The minarets are distinguished by multiple stages and carved balconies.
  • The cause of the reported vibration is not conclusively established.
  • Champaner Jama Masjid has 2 prominent central minarets; Nagina Masjid retains carved lower portions of minarets.
  • Trap: Do not identify Jhulta Minara as the Tree of Life jali of Sidi Saiyyed Mosque.

[Sources: Gujarat Tourism, Jhulta Minara Sidi Bashir Mosque Ahmedabad, About the Location, consulted 23 November 2026; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation Heritage Department, Jama Masjid, monument description, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Champaner and Pavagadh Archaeological Park, About the Place, consulted 23 November 2026; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 8, section Minars, printed pp. 113–114.]

body:
Historical setting

Champaner-Pavagadh is located in the Panchmahal district of Gujarat. The historic complex includes Champaner at the foot of Pavagadh Hill, as well as fortifications, religious monuments, residential remains and water structures.

The site's most important Indo-Islamic phase developed under Sultan Mahmud Begada of Gujarat. He captured Pavagadh in 1484 and subsequently developed Champaner as a capital.

Champaner's mosques belong to the regional Gujarat Sultanate tradition rather than the later mature Mughal imperial style. They demonstrate how Islamic architectural requirements were combined with the elaborate stone carving and structural traditions of the region.

Champaner Jama Masjid

The Jama Masjid of Champaner, also called Jami Masjid or the Great Mosque, is the most prominent mosque in the surviving Sultanate capital.

It stands just outside the eastern gate of the citadel. A richly carved entrance porch leads towards an open courtyard surrounded by pillared passages.

The western prayer hall contains multiple domes, carved stone columns, finely perforated screens and 2 tall central minarets.

An especially important identification fact is that the mosque has 7 mihrabs along its western prayer wall.

The building demonstrates Gujarat's architectural synthesis through the combination of an Islamic congregational plan with elaborate local stone carving, pillared spaces and decorative forms.

Other important mosques of Champaner

Saher ki Masjid

Saher ki Masjid stands inside the citadel. It is generally regarded as probably having served as a private royal mosque. The qualification matters because its exact original use is not established with the same certainty as its location.

Kevada or Kevda Masjid

Kevada Masjid is another important mosque of the Champaner complex. It contains a prayer structure with minarets and is associated with a nearby funerary monument or cenotaph.

Its combination of religious and funerary features demonstrates that mosques and commemorative structures could form related architectural groups.

Nagina Masjid

Nagina Masjid is distinguished by its finely carved stone ornamentation. A particularly important fact is that carved lower portions of minarets flank its central arch.

Exquisite geometric carving is also visible on the adjacent tomb. This makes Nagina Masjid a useful example of elaborate mosque and funerary stone carving.

Lila Gumbaj ki Masjid

Lila Gumbaj ki Masjid stands on a raised platform and is recognised by its fluted central dome. A fluted dome has visible curved ridges or channels that create a ribbed appearance.

Comparing Champaner's mosques

MosqueKey featureIdentification clue
Jama Masjid2 tall minarets and 7 mihrabsGreat congregational mosque near the citadel's eastern gate
Saher ki MasjidLocation inside the citadelProbably a private royal mosque
Kevada MasjidMinarets and nearby funerary structureMosque associated with a cenotaph
Nagina MasjidFine geometric carving; surviving minaret portionsAdjacent carved tomb
Lila Gumbaj ki MasjidFluted central domeRaised platform

The cultural importance of Champaner

Champaner is more than a collection of individual mosques. Its archaeological remains preserve evidence of a planned Sultanate capital, including religious buildings, royal spaces, fortifications and water systems.

The combination of these elements explains its importance as a historical urban site. The mosques are especially significant because their architecture demonstrates the regional interaction of Hindu and Islamic building traditions.

Prelims focus

  • Champaner-Pavagadh lies in Panchmahal district.
  • Mahmud Begada captured Pavagadh in 1484.
  • Champaner Jama Masjid has 2 tall central minarets and 7 mihrabs.
  • Saher ki Masjid is inside the citadel and was probably a royal mosque.
  • Nagina Masjid retains carved minaret portions; Lila Gumbaj ki Masjid has a fluted central dome.
  • Trap: Ahmedabad Jama Masjid's 260 columns and 15 domes should not be confused with Champaner Jama Masjid's 7 mihrabs.

[Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, Brief Synthesis and Criteria (iii)–(iv), consulted 23 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, History and Monuments, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Champaner and Pavagadh Archaeological Park, About the Place and Brief History, consulted 23 November 2026.]
